title: Tree: Level Order Traversal
directAnswer: Level order visits nodes top-to-bottom, left-to-right, one level at a time — a breadth-first search with a FIFO queue. Seed the queue with the root; repeatedly dequeue a node, print it, and enqueue its left then right children. The queue's FIFO property is what guarantees level order. It's O(n) time and O(w) space where w is the maximum width. To emit nodes grouped by level, snapshot the queue size at the start of each level and dequeue exactly that many.

remember.pattern: Breadth-first search with a FIFO queue
rules: Use a **FIFO queue** (enqueue at back, dequeue at front) — a stack would give DFS, not BFS.
Enqueue **left child before right** so each level prints left-to-right.
To group by level, **snapshot `queue.size()`** before the inner loop, then dequeue exactly that many.
Never enqueue null children — guard each enqueue, or you'll null-dereference on dequeue.
Space is O(w), the maximum level width — up to ~n/2 for the bottom level of a balanced tree.
whenToUse: You need nodes in top-down, left-to-right order
Per-level processing: right side view, level averages, zigzag, level sums
Shortest-path-style problems where the first time you reach a node is optimal (min depth)
antiSignals: You need sorted BST output → inorder DFS
You need root-before-children top-down recursion → preorder DFS
Memory is tight and the tree is wide → DFS uses O(h) instead of O(w)
remember.takeaway: Level order IS breadth-first search on a tree. The FIFO queue does all the work; the 'snapshot the size, drain exactly that many' idiom upgrades a flat traversal into per-level grouping and powers Right Side View, Zigzag, and Level Averages.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a queue (BFS) for level-by-level processing and can optionally group nodes by level with the size-snapshot trick.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using a stack instead of a queue (gives DFS), enqueuing null children, or reading queue.size() inside the inner loop so levels bleed together.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as BFS, explain why FIFO yields level order, and offer the size-snapshot grouping as the gateway to Right Side View and Zigzag.

problemStatement: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print its **level-order traversal**: the node values visited top-to-bottom and, within each level, left-to-right, separated by spaces.
constraints: Output values are space-separated in level-order sequence
understanding: Visit every node level by level: all nodes at depth 0, then all at depth 1, and so on, scanning each level left to right. This is breadth-first search, and a FIFO queue naturally produces exactly this order because nodes are dequeued in the same order they were enqueued.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Flat list or grouped by level?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: HackerRank prints a single flat line. LeetCode 102 wants a list of lists, one per level. The size-snapshot trick handles grouping; confirm which the interviewer wants.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Queue or stack?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Queue (FIFO). A stack would process the most recently added node first, producing a depth-first order instead of level order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Left or right child first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Enqueue the left child before the right so each level is printed left-to-right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the space cost?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: O(w), the maximum width of any level. For a balanced tree the widest level holds about half the nodes, so O(n) worst case — more than DFS's O(h).

approaches.name: BFS with a Queue — Flat Level Order (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here for the HackerRank single-line output. It's the canonical BFS.
hints: You want to process nodes in the order you first reach them, breadth-first. What data structure dequeues items in the same order they were added?
Seed a FIFO queue with the root. Each iteration: dequeue a node, print it, then enqueue its children.
Enqueue the left child before the right so each level comes out left-to-right. Guard against null children.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued once and dequeued once with O(1) work → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one-and-a-bit levels, bounded by the maximum width w → O(w) space.
approaches.explanation:
Level-order traversal is breadth-first search applied to a tree, and a FIFO queue produces it almost for free.

**Why FIFO yields level order.** Enqueue the root. When you dequeue it and enqueue its two children, the children go to the *back* of the queue — behind nothing, since the root was alone. When you dequeue those children and enqueue *their* children, the grandchildren land behind the rest of level 1. Because a queue preserves arrival order, you always finish an entire level before any node of the next level surfaces. That's the level-order guarantee, and it falls out of the FIFO discipline with no extra bookkeeping.

**Left before right.** Enqueuing the left child first means it's dequeued first, so within each level nodes come out left-to-right — the conventional reading order.

**Guard the null children.** Only enqueue children that actually exist. If you enqueued nulls, you'd later dequeue a null and dereference it for its children, crashing. The `if (child != null)` guard is not optional.

**Space is about width, not height.** Unlike DFS (whose stack is O(h)), BFS holds a whole level at once, so its space is O(w), the maximum width. For a balanced tree the last level has ~n/2 nodes, making BFS O(n) space in the worst case — a real trade-off to mention.
approaches.insight: A queue's FIFO order is the entire algorithm. You're not 'tracking levels' explicitly — the queue's arrival order does it for you. Recognizing 'process in arrival order = use a queue = BFS' is the transferable lesson.

approaches.name: BFS Grouped by Level — Size Snapshot
approaches.whenToMention: Use when the interviewer wants a list-of-lists (LeetCode 102) or per-level processing like right-side view or level averages.
hints: The flat BFS loses level boundaries. How can you tell where one level ends and the next begins, using only the queue?
At the start of each outer iteration, the queue holds exactly one complete level. Record its size before dequeuing anything.
Loop exactly `size` times to drain that level into a sublist, enqueuing children for the next level as you go.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Still each node enqueued and dequeued once → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level → O(w) space; the output list adds O(n).
approaches.explanation:
A flat BFS prints every node but erases the level boundaries. To recover them you exploit a simple invariant: **at the top of each outer-loop iteration, the queue contains exactly the nodes of one complete level.**

**Snapshot the size first.** Record `levelSize = queue.size()` before touching the queue. That count is precisely how many nodes are on the current level. Now dequeue *exactly* `levelSize` nodes, collecting their values into a sublist and enqueuing their children. Because you only loop `levelSize` times, you stop right at the level boundary — even though the queue has grown with the next level's children in the meantime.

**Why snapshot up front.** If you read `queue.size()` inside the loop instead, it would change as you enqueue children, and you'd bleed across level boundaries — the classic bug. Capturing it once freezes the boundary.

**Same complexity, richer output.** This costs nothing asymptotically over the flat version; you simply wrap each level's values in their own list. This exact 'snapshot the size, drain that many' skeleton is the foundation for Right Side View (take the last of each level), Zigzag (alternate the append direction), and Level Averages (mean per level).
approaches.insight: The queue size at the start of an iteration equals the current level's node count — freeze it before the inner loop and you get perfect per-level grouping. That one line is the difference between a flat traversal and the entire family of per-level tree problems.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stack instead of queue
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A stack pops the most recently added node, producing a depth-first order. Level order requires FIFO so the current level finishes before the next begins.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Size read inside the inner loop when grouping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Enqueuing children grows the queue mid-level. Reading the size inside the loop moves the boundary and merges levels.
